source: You decided to destroy your research.

Starting with the day you set out on this expedition, the ledger has been regularly updated with notes and results of your work at the digsite. The entries themselves are granular in detail, amounting to a read that isn't particularly interesting for the uninitiated.
You flip back to where the most crucial research was, half-expecting it to be there. Instead, you're only met by the jagged spines of the pages you tore out.

The rest of the entry specifies how such containment could be achieved, and mentions a small team of scientists being relocated to outside the Walls - led, of course, by you and Jorge.

Your conclusion was that the Artifact was too great a hazard to risk experimenting on further. It needed to be contained in order to prevent possible biochemical catastrophe. Bringing it into the City would be incredibly irresponsible..

Your conclusion was that the Artifact was too important to take risks with - that it needed to be secured in the City. The following paragraphs outline a series of guidelines and instructions regarding what type of containment, equipment, and personnel further experiments would require.

You can't help but feel a little sad as you tear page after page from the ledger. Eventually, the central conclusions have all been removed, with the only thing left being notes and updates leading up to a climax that no longer exists.

Nothing else catches your eye. If anything, the collected information in this ledger could be an incredibly handy guide for any future excavations of this type. After all, the two of you have made every mistake conceivable, as well as learned how to correct them.

Compared to your personal notes, the research ledgers are heavy and imposing, like a set of encyclopedias. Samples, notes, and a number of strange findings in plastic bags are stuck in and sheltered betwixt pages.
You open up the research again and are once more greeted by that familiar concoction of smells - hot plastic, hand sanitizer, dusty paper and leaded ink.
The research rests heavy on the makeshift workbench. It's almost monolithic in size and importance, and you hesitate for a moment before opening the ledger. The spine lets out a satisfying crack.

Towards the very end, however, mentions of the artifact start appearing. One entry in particular catches your attention, being ten times longer than most of the others. You wrote this on the first day of your experiments.
